intro: Look around your city. You will see churches, synagogues, mosques, temples and gurdwaras. You will meet classmates who pray in many ways, and some who do not follow a religion at all. Chicago is a place where many faiths live side by side.

In this unit you will visit houses of worship, learn about the 1893 Parliament of Religions, and see what the First Amendment says about freedom of religion. You will also hear how some faiths are kept by telling stories, and how faiths traveled with people to Chicago.
By the end, you will be able to name houses of worship, explain freedom of religion in plain words, ask kind questions, and tell how faiths change and grow when people move.
bigQuestion: How do people of many faiths share one community, and how do their faiths travel and grow?

timeline.t: Anishinaabe nations live around the Great Lakes and pass on stories by telling
The First Amendment protects freedom of religion in the United States
Immigrants from Europe build churches and synagogues in Chicago
Chicago hosts the World's Parliament of Religions
The Great Migration begins; Black churches grow on Chicago's South Side
Gospel music grows in Chicago churches, led by Thomas A. Dorsey
The Bahá'í House of Worship in Wilmette opens for worship
A new law lets more immigrants come from Asia and Africa
The Parliament of the World's Religions meets again in Chicago

test.q: Where do Muslims often gather to pray?
test.why: Muslims often pray together in a mosque.

test.q: What does the First Amendment protect?
choices: Freedom of religion, including no religion
test.why: The First Amendment keeps the government from picking a religion and lets people follow any faith or none.

test.q: What was special about 1893 in Chicago?
choices: The World's Parliament of Religions met
test.why: The World's Parliament of Religions met in Chicago in 1893.

test.q: Which building in Wilmette has nine doors?
test.why: The Bahá'í House of Worship has nine sides and nine doors and welcomes all.

choices: Teachings passed down by speaking and remembering
test.why: An oral tradition is passed down by telling, singing and remembering.

test.q: Why might an elder ask you not to retell a story?
choices: It may be sacred and kept within the community
test.why: Some stories are sacred and meant only for the community, so learners ask permission.

test.q: In many Anishinaabe stories, what is Turtle Island?
test.why: Many Native people call North America Turtle Island, from a creation story.
Many followers of Yoruba religion honor the orishas as powerful spirits.

test.q: Which word is Jewish giving to people in need?
test.why: Tzedakah is the Jewish word for giving as a matter of justice. Zakat is the Muslim word.

test.q: What did the Great Migration bring to Chicago?
choices: Many Black churches and gospel music
test.why: Black families from the South built churches, and gospel music grew there.

test.q: Which is a respectful question about a classmate's holiday?
choices: How does your family celebrate it?
test.why: Asking how a family celebrates is kind and open. The others tease.

test.q: Which tradition grew in Brazil from Yoruba roots?
test.why: Candomblé grew in Brazil from Yoruba roots. Santería grew in Cuba.

test.q: What may a public school do about religion?
test.why: Public schools may teach about religions but may not tell students what to believe.

test.q: What change in 1965 helped bring more temples and mosques to Chicago?
test.why: A 1965 law let more people come from Asia and Africa, who built new houses of worship.

test.q: Which three nations form the Council of Three Fires?
test.why: The Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi call themselves Anishinaabe and form the Council of Three Fires.

write.prompt: How can people of different faiths be good neighbors? Use two or three sources from this unit, such as Leviticus 19:34, Matthew 7:12 and the First Amendment. Explain what each source says and how it could help neighbors live and work together.
tips: Say who believes what: "Christians believe..." or "The Torah teaches..."
Compare the sources. Do not say one faith is better.
Use words from the unit, like interfaith and freedom of religion.
End with one idea you would try in your own school.
